j.thinking_skill: moves her body in time to a drum beat
j.notes: Nothing is taught: the 'shop for ingredients tomorrow' line dangles and 'her ear perked up at that word' refers to no word; the story is just dancing with a bolted-on 'learning something new' refrain.

j.learned_fact: Claims that sleeping squishes the soft parts of your back so you are shorter in the morning; this is false (spinal discs rehydrate overnight, so people are tallest in the morning and shorter by evening).
j.thinking_skill: reasons by analogy from a squishable toy to his own back
j.notes: Internally contradictory: he fails to reach the line in the morning, then 'in the morning the soft parts got big again' and he reaches it; the science is backwards and 'Brooks was sorry he was tired' is garbled.

j.learned_fact: No matter how many handfuls or tally marks you have, you can always add one more (counting never ends).
j.thinking_skill: generalizes a repeated action into a rule (there is always one more)
j.notes: The knock at the door is an unrelated ending, and the 'that is the most' moment is abrupt; the successor idea is sound but the bowl overflowing with chips is never resolved.

j.learned_fact: To learn a drum part: listen to the beat, hold the sticks firmly but not too tight, practise slowly then fast, then play it through.
j.thinking_skill: follows a sequence of steps in order
j.notes: First/Next/Then/Last scaffolding is mechanical and the 'learning' is a generic practice sequence; the flashlight-waving girl is an odd detail.

j.learned_fact: 7+5=12 and 9+3=12; twelve can be split into two equal groups of six with none left over.
j.thinking_skill: notices that different pairs make the same total and that it splits evenly
j.notes: Teacher-directed First/Next/Then/Last steps make it feel like a worksheet; 'rocky bowl' and 'with a wink' are forced insertions.

j.learned_fact: Rubbing a balloon on your hair makes it stick to a wall and makes your hair stand up toward it (static electricity is shown but not named).
j.thinking_skill: repeats an action and observes a stronger effect (more rubbing, better sticking)
j.notes: Setting is incoherent (a wall and a mirror in a park, then a 'hike' home) and the closing 'by following each step in order she had learned something real' is a bolted-on moral with no explanation of why the balloon sticks.

j.learned_fact: Elephants send messages to each other with long, low rumbles that travel through the ground and are too low for humans to hear; a story, an advertisement and an information page serve different purposes.
j.thinking_skill: classifies three texts by purpose to judge which is trustworthy
j.notes: Norah feels the elephants' rumble 'through the floor under her feet' while watching a video, which is impossible; the text-type segment is a librarian quiz rather than story.

j.learned_fact: Two rectangles with the same area (3x4 and 2x6, both 12 square metres) can have different perimeters (14 m vs 16 m); a long thin shape needs more fence.
j.thinking_skill: compares two cases holding area constant to isolate the effect of shape on perimeter
j.notes: Forced sensory/vocabulary padding ('delicious apple' eaten mid-lesson, 'her humor made Parker smile' though nothing funny happened, coffee-and-cinnamon teacher) undercuts an otherwise correct maths moment.

j.learned_fact: States the Titanic 'had only 1,178 lifeboats' and that this is 'way less than half' of 2,224 people. Both false: Titanic had 20 lifeboats with a total capacity of about 1,178 people, and 1,178 is more than half of 2,224.
j.thinking_skill: compares two quantities to judge whether one is sufficient
j.notes: The central fact is wrong twice over (lifeboat count vs capacity, and the arithmetic), and the character's 'why only about half' contradicts her own 'way less than half'; the octopus-song opening is filler.

j.learned_fact: When rolling two dice, a total of seven comes up more often than any other total (34 of 200 rolls here), while 2 and 12 are rarest.
j.thinking_skill: tests a hunch empirically by tallying 200 trials
j.notes: Vocabulary is misused ('Seven is the criterion', 'notorious for being unfair'), the design conclusion does not follow (bonus squares at 7, 14, 21 on a cumulative track are not reached by single-roll sums), and grandma's 'took mathematicians hundreds of years' overclaims.

j.learned_fact: Overmixing once flour is added makes cookies dense and tough; folding the flour in gently keeps shortbread tender and crumbly.
j.thinking_skill: runs a controlled comparison changing one variable (mixing force)
j.notes: Target words are jammed in nonsensically ('reach the climax of the recipe', 'it wasn't a voluntary choice', 'sustain'); the explanation of why (gluten development) is never given, so the mechanism stays vague.

j.learned_fact: Wrapping an object in a wet cloth and putting it in moving air cools it as the water evaporates (evaporative cooling).
j.thinking_skill: applies a hypothesis and monitors the result over time
j.notes: Premise is shaky (insulin does not spoil in two hours at room temperature) and forced words ('admittedly extravagant', 'plague of interactive exhibits', 'excavate from an ancient tomb') read as vocabulary quota rather than narrative.

j.learned_fact: Only about 2.5% of Earth's water is fresh, most of that is locked in glaciers and ice sheets, and under 1% is readily accessible.
j.thinking_skill: revises a confident wrong estimate against data and re-explains it as nested fractions
j.notes: Explicitly set in an 'eighth-grade science class' with middle-school prose although the target is 9th grade; 'synthesis' and 'profound' are inserted rather than used.

j.learned_fact: Lithium batteries lose capacity faster when kept at full charge or in heat; storing one at about 50% in a cool place preserves it for years.
j.thinking_skill: revises a model by adding variables after a counterexample
j.notes: 'My predecessor model' is a misuse and 'the ethical choice to build something honest' is a bolted-on moral; the story also blurs daily charge drain with long-term capacity fade.

j.learned_fact: Sound travels about 343 m/s, so counting the seconds between lightning and thunder and dividing by three gives the distance in kilometres.
j.thinking_skill: plans a controlled experiment changing a single variable
j.notes: The thunder digression is a non sequitur bolted onto the bread plot, and the logic is muddled: she says she changed only one thing and everything failed, then resolves to change only one thing; 'apathetic about the math', 'fathom' and 'retarded' are forced.

j.learned_fact: In 1976 Appel and Haken proved the four colour theorem (any planar map needs at most four colours) by having a computer check nearly two thousand cases, which sparked debate over whether a computer-checked proof counts as proof.
j.thinking_skill: tests a conjecture against adversarial cases and questions what counts as proof
j.notes: Mr. Chen delivers the history as a mini-lecture and says 'exactly four' where 'at most four' is correct; 'vehement', 'heresy' and 'relegated' are visibly planted.

j.learned_fact: Akerlof's 1970 'lemons' analysis: when buyers cannot tell good used cars from bad, they offer average prices, owners of good cars withdraw, and quality and prices spiral down (adverse selection from information asymmetry).
j.thinking_skill: reasons about a system-level outcome emerging from individually rational choices, holding two truths at once
j.notes: Minor slips only: 'the monotony of market collapse' is a misuse and 'a economist' is a typo; the ending is a touch heavy on abstraction.

j.learned_fact: Drained peatland keeps releasing carbon for decades as the peat oxidises; disturbing it with construction accelerates that release and can outweigh the carbon stored in the trees above it.
j.thinking_skill: revises an analysis after discovering an omitted factor
j.notes: Opens with a markdown title, cast is 'mostly seniors' for an 11th-grade target, and 'promulgate' and 'disparate' (twice) are forced; 'decades or centuries of worth in a single season' is garbled.

j.learned_fact: GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day faster than ground clocks because of relativity; without correcting for it, position errors would grow by kilometres each day.
j.thinking_skill: integrates an abstract principle into a conceptual framework
j.notes: The physics arrives as a brother's monologue rather than through Lily's own inquiry; 'quiescent' and 'the solvency of the system' are misplaced vocabulary.

j.learned_fact: GPS satellite clocks run about 38 microseconds a day fast because of relativity; uncorrected, this would produce position errors growing by kilometres each day.
j.thinking_skill: connects a researched principle to an observed symptom to diagnose a bug
j.notes: The debugging premise is implausible: a beginner's phone-GPS script would never contain the relativistic clock correction, and the symptom (wild second-to-second jumps, kilometres in minutes) does not match slow daily drift; 'the mesmerize quality' is ungrammatical.

j.learned_fact: A correlation coefficient near zero only means no straight-line relationship; a curved inverted-U relationship (free-throw accuracy rising then falling with hours trained) can hide behind r near 0.
j.thinking_skill: reinterprets a null result by hypothesising a nonlinear model and re-plotting the data
j.notes: She re-plots per-hour data she never said she collected, and 'diaphanous quality of his focus' and 'commodify my time' are planted vocabulary; otherwise a solid, well-paced statistics story.
